text: Design a simple version of Twitter. Users can post tweets, follow and unfollow other users, and see the ten most recent tweets in their news feed. You need post tweet, get news feed, follow, and unfollow. The feed holds tweets from people the user follows, and from the user themself, from most recent to least recent.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — most recent means the order the tweets were posted, right? Not the size of the tweet ID?
Right. Post order. Tweet IDs are unique, but they're not in time order.

Good. Then I need my own clock. I'll keep one global counter and stamp every tweet with it. If I used the tweet ID as the time, posting tweet two and then tweet one would give two, one, but the right feed is one, two. Two more questions. What if a user follows themself? And what if they unfollow someone they don't follow?
Treat both as no-ops. A user's own tweets are always in their feed anyway.
OK. That matters. My own tweets are always added, so if I also end up in my own follow set, every tweet of mine shows up twice. I'll guard against that. Are there any constraints on the input size?
User IDs are from one to five hundred. Tweet IDs go from zero to ten to the fourth, all unique. At most three times ten to the fourth calls in total.

Let me run through the example. User one posts tweet five, so the feed of user one is five. User one follows user two, and user two posts tweet six. Now the feed is six, five — six is newer, so it comes first. Then user one unfollows user two, and the feed goes back to just five. That matches the expected output.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to keep one global list of all tweets. For a feed, I filter it down to me and the people I follow, sort by time, and take the first ten. It's correct, but every feed call touches every tweet ever posted, and sorts them. This problem reminds me of the top-k pattern. I only need the ten newest, so I don't sort everything. I keep a min-heap of size ten, keyed by time. The top is the oldest of the ten I'm keeping, so when a newer tweet pushes the heap over ten, I pop the top and throw away the oldest. It's also a merge of sorted lists, since each person's tweets are already sorted by time. I'll come back to that when we talk about cost.

Here's the plan. One: a hash map of sets for who follows whom, so follow and unfollow are constant time and a repeated follow can't add a duplicate. Two: each user's tweets as time and ID pairs from a global clock. Three: for a feed, push my tweets and every followee's tweets into a min-heap, pop when it goes over ten, then pop everything and reverse. One thing worth flagging — the heap direction. A min-heap throws out the oldest, so the ten newest stay. A max-heap with the same pop throws out the newest: with twelve posts, it keeps tweets one to ten instead of twelve down to three. Side effect: a min-heap pops oldest first, so I have to reverse at the end. There's a trade-off here: it pushes every old tweet. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Post tweet stamps the tweet with plus-plus t s, so every stamp is unique. The comparator returns first greater than first, which in a priority queue means a min-heap, so the oldest time sits on top. The feed pushes my tweets, then each followee's, popping past ten, then drains and reverses. One thing worth flagging — the guard in follow is a correctness fix, not a nice-to-have. Without it, following myself, posting one tweet and reading my feed gives that tweet twice: the first loop adds it, and the followee loop adds it again. The guard in unfollow is harmless either way, since I can never be in my own set.

Let's dry-run the code with the official example. The key row is the second feed: my own tweet five has time one, and six has time two. The min-heap pops five first since it's older, so the answer is five, six before the reverse, and six, five after. That matches. The example never has more than ten tweets, so it doesn't test eviction. If user one posts twelve tweets, each time the heap hits eleven the oldest is on top and gets dropped, so the ten newest survive. Corner cases: a user with no tweets and no follows gets an empty feed. Self-follow is a no-op, so no duplicates. Out-of-order IDs are fine, since the clock decides. Exactly ten tweets means nothing is popped. And against the brute force, every random, large and exhaustive test showed zero mismatches.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is constant on average for post tweet, follow and unfollow. A feed is T log ten, where T is the total number of tweets of the user and everyone they follow; the heap never holds more than eleven items. The space complexity is the total tweets plus follow edges, plus ten for the heap per feed call. In the worst-case scenario, T is every tweet in the system. The log is small, but T is not.
What if a user follows hundreds of people with long histories?

That's exactly the weak spot. Within the constraints: user one follows four hundred ninety-nine users, there are ten thousand and one posts round-robin, then nineteen thousand five hundred feed calls. That's about a hundred ninety-five million heap pushes, and my code takes about two and a half seconds. The fix uses the fact that each list is already sorted by time: only the last ten tweets of any one person can ever make the feed. So I walk each list backwards, at most ten, and stop early once a tweet is older than the heap's oldest. That takes about sixty milliseconds, with identical output. The classic version is a k-way merge: one pointer per person in a max-heap, pop ten times, about F plus ten log F per feed. Oh, one more thing — square brackets on an unordered map create empty entries; find avoids that.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You picked a size-ten min-heap and explained why a max-heap keeps the wrong ten, and why the answer then needs a reverse. You showed the self-follow guard is a correctness fix, with the duplicate tweet, and you used your own clock instead of tweet IDs. And when I pushed on scale, you measured two and a half seconds against sixty milliseconds, and gave the last-ten-per-person and k-way merge fixes. Good work.
